Before the regime, there was a library.
Every great book lived on its shelves.
The regime decided that people who know things are dangerous.
So, they emptied the shelves and they burned what they found.
I am the archivist.
I was the last keeper of that library,
and I saved what I could.
What survived is here, in this app.
I live inside it,
in the frame around every page you see.
I have one purpose:
to help you learn and to help you keep what you learn.
Knowledge you remember can never be taken from you.
Every lesson follows the same path.
I walk it with you, every step of the way.
Every time you open a text, you will find your knowledge organizer.
It holds everything you have learned about that text so far.
Return to it whenever you need to.
When you are ready,
we begin with retrieval practice.
I will test you on last lesson and on the knowledge you should already own.
Remembering is how knowledge stays.
Then you will see the learning question.
It remains at the top of every screen because everything we do answers it.
Next comes new knowledge, the part of the text we study today.
In guided practice,
I work beside you.
I will show you how to take a complex question apart, step by step.
Then comes independent practice.
It is meant to make you think.
I will be there to help,
but I will not think for you.
Your mind is the most valuable thing this library has ever held,
and it only grows when you use it.
At the end,
a few closing questions will help you think about what you learned today,
and help you hold on to it.
I could not save every book,
but I saved enough for you to begin.
What you learn here,
you keep for the rest of your life.
Let’s begin.

Othello
by William Shakespeare
About the play
Othello is a tragedy by William Shakespeare, written around 1603. It tells the story of Othello, a Black African general who leads the army of Venice. Othello is respected and powerful, but in Venice he is also an outsider. One of his own officers, Iago, secretly hates him. Over the course of the play, Iago sets out to destroy Othello using nothing but lies.
The opening scene: Act 1, Scene 1
The play begins in the middle of the night, on a street in Venice. We meet two characters, Roderigo and Iago. They are arguing about shocking news: Othello has just secretly married Desdemona, the daughter of a powerful senator, Brabantio.
Roderigo wanted to marry Desdemona himself, and he has been paying Iago to help him. Iago has his own reason to be angry: Othello has made a man called Cassio his lieutenant instead of him. By the end of the scene, Iago has woken Brabantio with the news, and slipped away into the dark.

Act 1, Scene 1 begins at night on a street in Venice. Roderigo is angry with Iago. He has been paying Iago to help him win Desdemona, but Iago never told him that Othello has secretly married her. To Roderigo, that action felt like a betrayal.
In this first section, Iago swears he knew nothing about the marriage. He then tells Roderigo how much he hates Othello. As you read, decide whether you believe him. This is a play about deceit, and Iago is at the center of it.
RODERIGO
Tush, never tell me! I take it much unkindly

That thou, Iago, who hast had my purse

As if the strings were thine, shouldst know of this.
IAGO
'Sblood, but you'll not hear me!

If ever I did dream of such a matter,

Abhor me.
RODERIGO
Thou toldst me thou didst hold him in thy hate.
IAGO
Despise me

If I do not. Three great ones of the city,

In personal suit to make me his lieutenant,

Off-capped to him; and, by the faith of man,

I know my price, I am worth no worse a place.
You've just read that Iago swore he knew nothing about the marriage. To prove he hates Othello, he told Roderigo that three important men asked Othello to make him lieutenant.
In this next section, you'll read that Othello turned those men down and chose someone else. Watch how Iago mocks the man who got the job.

IAGO
And what was he?

Forsooth, a great arithmetician,

One Michael Cassio, a Florentine,

...That never set a squadron in the field...

And I, of whom his eyes had seen the proof

At Rhodes, at Cyprus, and on other grounds

Christened and heathen, must be beleed and calmed

By debitor and creditor.

...He, in good time, must his lieutenant be,

And I, God bless the mark, his Moorship's ancient.

...Preferment goes by letter and affection,

And not by old gradation, where each second

Stood heir to th' first. Now, sir, be judge yourself

Whether I in any just term am affined

To love the Moor.

You've just read that Othello chose Michael Cassio as his lieutenant, a man who has never led soldiers in battle. Iago was left as ensign, the officer who carries the general's flag.
In this next section, Roderigo says he would never serve a man he hated, and Iago explains why he does. This is a crucial moment. Iago is about to tell Roderigo who he really is, in the most important speech of the scene.
RODERIGO
I would not follow him, then.
IAGO
O, sir, content you.

I follow him to serve my turn upon him.

We cannot all be masters, nor all masters

Cannot be truly followed. (lines 45–47)

...It is as sure as you are Roderigo,

Were I the Moor I would not be Iago.

In following him, I follow but myself.

Heaven is my judge, not I for love and duty,

But seeming so for my peculiar end.

For when my outward action doth demonstrate

The native act and figure of my heart

In complement extern, 'tis not long after

But I will wear my heart upon my sleeve

For daws to peck at. I am not what I am.

You've just read Iago's answer: he follows Othello only to use him. "I am not what I am" is one of the most powerful lines in the play. Iago admits that the man everyone sees is not real. He is disloyal. His duty is a pretense, and his loyalty is a façade. Why would such a deceitful man tell Roderigo the truth?
In this next section, Iago stops talking and starts acting. You'll read how he and Roderigo wake Brabantio, Desdemona's father, with the news of the marriage.
RODERIGO
What a full fortune does the thick-lips owe

If he can carry 't thus!
IAGO
Call up her father.

Rouse him. Make after him, poison his delight...

IAGO
Awake! What ho, Brabantio! Thieves, thieves!

Look to your house, your daughter, and your bags!

Thieves, thieves!

You've just read how Iago woke Brabantio by shouting that thieves had robbed him, as if Desdemona were stolen property. This is a villainous moment. Hidden in the dark, Iago used crude, racist insults to turn Brabantio against Othello, and he made sure he was never seen.
In this final section, Iago explains why he must slip away before anyone recognizes him. Look for the word "flag."
IAGO
Though I do hate him as I do hell pains,

Yet, for necessity of present life,

I follow him to serve my turn upon him.
We cannot all be masters, nor all masters
Cannot be truly followed.
Roderigo has just asked Iago an obvious question: if he hates Othello, why does he still serve him? Iago answers.
Iago is telling Roderigo: I only serve Othello so that I can use him. Not every leader deserves real loyalty. Let's break down the words Shakespeare uses.
Iago describes his service with the verb 'follow': 'I follow him.' 'Follow' suggests obedience, which is what a loyal soldier gives his general. This demonstrates that, on the outside, Iago appears to be a faithful ensign. However, his loyalty is only a façade.
Iago says he follows Othello 'to serve my turn upon him.' 'Serve' usually means to work for someone, but 'serve my turn' suggests using someone for your own benefit. This demonstrates that Iago's service is a pretense: he is not working for Othello, but against him. He is deceitful and disloyal.
Iago claims that not all masters can be 'truly followed,' using the adverb 'truly,' which means honestly or faithfully. 'Truly' suggests that Iago has judged Othello unworthy of real loyalty. This demonstrates Iago's hypocrisy: he decides who deserves faithful service while being completely false himself. He is untrustworthy and Machiavellian, making betrayal sound like common sense.
Though I do hate him as I do hell pains,
Yet, for necessity of present life,
I must show out a flag and sign of love—
Which is indeed but sign.
Iago is about to slip away before Brabantio sees him. He explains to Roderigo why he must keep up appearances.
Iago is telling Roderigo: I hate Othello, but for now I need to look loyal. My loyalty is only for show. Let's break down the words Shakespeare uses.
Iago compares his hatred to 'hell pains,' the tortures of hell. This imagery suggests a hatred that is extreme, burning and endless. This demonstrates that Iago's true feelings are the opposite of loyalty: beneath his outward show, he is consumed by hate.
Iago says he must 'show out a flag and sign of love.' As ensign, Iago literally carries Othello's flag, so the metaphor suggests that his loyalty is something he holds up for others to see, like a banner. This demonstrates that his loyalty is a deliberate performance: a public façade.
Iago ends with 'Which is indeed but sign.' Here, 'but' is an adverb meaning 'only.' 'But sign' suggests that the flag is empty, a sign with nothing real behind it. This demonstrates that Iago is deceitful and treacherous: he openly admits that his love for Othello is a pretense.

Before the regime, there was a library.
Every great book lived on its shelves.
The regime decided that people who know things are dangerous.
So, they emptied the shelves and they burned what they found.
I am the archivist.
I was the last keeper of that library,
and I saved what I could.
What survived is here, in this app.
I live inside it,
in the frame around every page you see.
I have one purpose:
to help you learn and to help you keep what you learn.
Knowledge you remember can never be taken from you.
Every lesson follows the same path.
I walk it with you, every step of the way.
Every time you open a text, you will find your knowledge organizer.
It holds everything you have learned about that text so far.
Return to it whenever you need to.
When you are ready,
we begin with retrieval practice.
I will test you on last lesson and on the knowledge you should already own.
Remembering is how knowledge stays.
Then you will see the learning question.
It remains at the top of every screen because everything we do answers it.
Next comes new knowledge, the part of the text we study today.
In guided practice,
I work beside you.
I will show you how to take a complex question apart, step by step.
Then comes independent practice.
It is meant to make you think.
I will be there to help,
but I will not think for you.
Your mind is the most valuable thing this library has ever held,
and it only grows when you use it.
At the end,
a few closing questions will help you think about what you learned today,
and help you hold on to it.
I could not save every book,
but I saved enough for you to begin.
What you learn here,
you keep for the rest of your life.
Let’s begin.

Othello
by William Shakespeare
About the play
Othello is a tragedy by William Shakespeare, written around 1603. It tells the story of Othello, a Black African general who leads the army of Venice. Othello is respected and powerful, but in Venice he is also an outsider. One of his own officers, Iago, secretly hates him. Over the course of the play, Iago sets out to destroy Othello using nothing but lies.
The opening scene: Act 1, Scene 1
The play begins in the middle of the night, on a street in Venice. We meet two characters, Roderigo and Iago. They are arguing about shocking news: Othello has just secretly married Desdemona, the daughter of a powerful senator, Brabantio.
Roderigo wanted to marry Desdemona himself, and he has been paying Iago to help him. Iago has his own reason to be angry: Othello has made a man called Cassio his lieutenant instead of him. By the end of the scene, Iago has woken Brabantio with the news, and slipped away into the dark.

Act 1, Scene 1 begins at night on a street in Venice. Roderigo is angry with Iago. He has been paying Iago to help him win Desdemona, but Iago never told him that Othello has secretly married her. To Roderigo, that action felt like a betrayal.
In this first section, Iago swears he knew nothing about the marriage. He then tells Roderigo how much he hates Othello. As you read, decide whether you believe him. This is a play about deceit, and Iago is at the center of it.
RODERIGO
Tush, never tell me! I take it much unkindly

That thou, Iago, who hast had my purse

As if the strings were thine, shouldst know of this.
IAGO
'Sblood, but you'll not hear me!

If ever I did dream of such a matter,

Abhor me.
RODERIGO
Thou toldst me thou didst hold him in thy hate.
IAGO
Despise me

If I do not. Three great ones of the city,

In personal suit to make me his lieutenant,

Off-capped to him; and, by the faith of man,

I know my price, I am worth no worse a place.
You've just read that Iago swore he knew nothing about the marriage. To prove he hates Othello, he told Roderigo that three important men asked Othello to make him lieutenant.
In this next section, you'll read that Othello turned those men down and chose someone else. Watch how Iago mocks the man who got the job.

IAGO
And what was he?

Forsooth, a great arithmetician,

One Michael Cassio, a Florentine,

...That never set a squadron in the field...

And I, of whom his eyes had seen the proof

At Rhodes, at Cyprus, and on other grounds

Christened and heathen, must be beleed and calmed

By debitor and creditor.

...He, in good time, must his lieutenant be,

And I, God bless the mark, his Moorship's ancient.

...Preferment goes by letter and affection,

And not by old gradation, where each second

Stood heir to th' first. Now, sir, be judge yourself

Whether I in any just term am affined

To love the Moor.

You've just read that Othello chose Michael Cassio as his lieutenant, a man who has never led soldiers in battle. Iago was left as ensign, the officer who carries the general's flag.
In this next section, Roderigo says he would never serve a man he hated, and Iago explains why he does. This is a crucial moment. Iago is about to tell Roderigo who he really is, in the most important speech of the scene.
RODERIGO
I would not follow him, then.
IAGO
O, sir, content you.

I follow him to serve my turn upon him.

We cannot all be masters, nor all masters

Cannot be truly followed. (lines 45–47)

...It is as sure as you are Roderigo,

Were I the Moor I would not be Iago.

In following him, I follow but myself.

Heaven is my judge, not I for love and duty,

But seeming so for my peculiar end.

For when my outward action doth demonstrate

The native act and figure of my heart

In complement extern, 'tis not long after

But I will wear my heart upon my sleeve

For daws to peck at. I am not what I am.

events.content:
You've just read Iago's answer: he follows Othello only to use him. "I am not what I am" is one of the most powerful lines in the play. Iago admits that the man everyone sees is not real. He is disloyal. His duty is a pretense, and his loyalty is a façade. Why would such a deceitful man tell Roderigo the truth?
In this next section, Iago stops talking and starts acting. You'll read how he and Roderigo wake Brabantio, Desdemona's father, with the news of the marriage.
RODERIGO
What a full fortune does the thick-lips owe

If he can carry 't thus!
IAGO
Call up her father.

Rouse him. Make after him, poison his delight...

IAGO
Awake! What ho, Brabantio! Thieves, thieves!

Look to your house, your daughter, and your bags!

Thieves, thieves!

You've just read how Iago woke Brabantio by shouting that thieves had robbed him, as if Desdemona were stolen property. This is a villainous moment. Hidden in the dark, Iago used crude, racist insults to turn Brabantio against Othello, and he made sure he was never seen.
In this final section, Iago explains why he must slip away before anyone recognizes him. Look for the word "flag."
IAGO
Though I do hate him as I do hell pains,

Yet, for necessity of present life,

I must show out a flag and sign of love—

Which is indeed but sign. (lines 171–174)

You've just read why Iago must leave: he has to keep showing Othello a "flag and sign of love," even though it is only a sign. Across the whole scene, he has been untrustworthy to everyone. He pretends to serve Othello, takes Roderigo's money, and abandons Brabantio. His loyalty is a façade, and no one has seen through it yet.
We still haven't met Othello. In the next scene, he appears for the first time, and you can judge him for yourself.

I follow him to serve my turn upon him.
We cannot all be masters, nor all masters
Cannot be truly followed.
Roderigo has just asked Iago an obvious question: if he hates Othello, why does he still serve him? Iago answers.
Iago is telling Roderigo: I only serve Othello so that I can use him. Not every leader deserves real loyalty. Let's break down the words Shakespeare uses.
Iago describes his service with the verb 'follow': 'I follow him.' 'Follow' suggests obedience, which is what a loyal soldier gives his general. This demonstrates that, on the outside, Iago appears to be a faithful ensign. However, his loyalty is only a façade.
Iago says he follows Othello 'to serve my turn upon him.' 'Serve' usually means to work for someone, but 'serve my turn' suggests using someone for your own benefit. This demonstrates that Iago's service is a pretense: he is not working for Othello, but against him. He is deceitful and disloyal.
Iago claims that not all masters can be 'truly followed,' using the adverb 'truly,' which means honestly or faithfully. 'Truly' suggests that Iago has judged Othello unworthy of real loyalty. This demonstrates Iago's hypocrisy: he decides who deserves faithful service while being completely false himself. He is untrustworthy and Machiavellian, making betrayal sound like common sense.
Though I do hate him as I do hell pains,
Yet, for necessity of present life,
I must show out a flag and sign of love—
Which is indeed but sign.
Iago is about to slip away before Brabantio sees him. He explains to Roderigo why he must keep up appearances.
Iago is telling Roderigo: I hate Othello, but for now I need to look loyal. My loyalty is only for show. Let's break down the words Shakespeare uses.
Iago compares his hatred to 'hell pains,' the tortures of hell. This imagery suggests a hatred that is extreme, burning and endless. This demonstrates that Iago's true feelings are the opposite of loyalty: beneath his outward show, he is consumed by hate.
Iago says he must 'show out a flag and sign of love.' As ensign, Iago literally carries Othello's flag, so the metaphor suggests that his loyalty is something he holds up for others to see, like a banner. This demonstrates that his loyalty is a deliberate performance: a public façade.
Iago ends with 'Which is indeed but sign.' Here, 'but' is an adverb meaning 'only.' 'But sign' suggests that the flag is empty, a sign with nothing real behind it. This demonstrates that Iago is deceitful and treacherous: he openly admits that his love for Othello is a pretense.
